title: Group Actions

The notion of a group “acting” on a set underlies much of mathematics. When we study symmetries of geometric objects, permutations of the roots of a polynomial, or even the structure of a group itself, we are studying group actions. Understanding which sets a group $G$ acts on, and how, gives information about $G$. These ideas return throughout the book: in Chapter 11 actions are the main tool for analyzing finite groups, and in representation theory groups act on vector spaces by linear maps.

## <span class="num">3.2.1</span> Actions, Orbits, and Stabilizers

:::definition{3.2.1} Group action
A ***(left) action*** of a group $G$ on a set $X$ is a map $G \times X \to X$, written $(g, x) \mapsto g \cdot x$, satisfying:

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. $e \cdot x = x$ for all $x \in X$;
2. $(gh) \cdot x = g \cdot (h \cdot x)$ for all $g, h \in G$ and $x \in X$.

We say $G$ ***acts on*** $X$, or that $X$ is a ***$G$-set***.
:::

Recall (Definition [2.2.8](/notes/math-55a/2-2-fundamental-examples#definition-2-2-8)) that $\Sym(X)$ denotes the group of all bijections $X \to X$ under composition.

:::proposition{3.2.2} Actions are homomorphisms to $\Sym(X)$
Given an action of $G$ on $X$, each map $\rho(g) : X \to X$, $x \mapsto g \cdot x$, is a bijection, and $\rho : G \to \Sym(X)$ is a homomorphism. Conversely, every homomorphism $\rho : G \to \Sym(X)$ defines an action by $g \cdot x = \rho(g)(x)$.
:::

:::proof
By the two axioms, $\rho(g)(\rho(g^{-1})(x)) = (gg^{-1}) \cdot x = e \cdot x = x$, and likewise $\rho(g^{-1})(\rho(g)(x)) = x$. So $\rho(g)$ is a bijection with inverse $\rho(g^{-1})$. The second axiom says $\rho(gh) = \rho(g) \circ \rho(h)$, so $\rho$ is a homomorphism. Conversely, if $\rho$ is a homomorphism, then $\rho(e) = \id_X$ gives $e \cdot x = x$, and $\rho(gh) = \rho(g) \circ \rho(h)$ gives $(gh) \cdot x = g \cdot (h \cdot x)$.
:::

So a group action is the same thing as a homomorphism from $G$ to a group of permutations. In Chapter 13 we replace $\Sym(X)$ by the group of invertible linear maps of a vector space; such homomorphisms are the *representations* of $G$ (Definition [13.1.1](/notes/math-55a/13-1-representations-and-subrepresentations#definition-13-1-1)).

:::definition{3.2.3} Orbits and stabilizers
Let $G$ act on $X$ and let $x \in X$.

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. The ***orbit*** of $x$ is $G \cdot x = \{g \cdot x \mid g \in G\} \subseteq X$, also written $\mathcal{O}_x$.
2. The ***stabilizer*** of $x$ is $\Stab(x) = \{g \in G \mid g \cdot x = x\} \subseteq G$.
:::

:::proposition{3.2.4} Stabilizers are subgroups
For any $x \in X$, the stabilizer $\Stab(x)$ is a subgroup of $G$.
:::

:::proof
We have $e \in \Stab(x)$ since $e \cdot x = x$. If $g, h \in \Stab(x)$, then $(gh) \cdot x = g \cdot (h \cdot x) = g \cdot x = x$, so $gh \in \Stab(x)$. If $g \in \Stab(x)$, then $x = e \cdot x = (g^{-1}g) \cdot x = g^{-1} \cdot (g \cdot x) = g^{-1} \cdot x$, so $g^{-1} \in \Stab(x)$.
:::

:::proposition{3.2.5} Orbits partition $X$
Define $x \sim y$ if $y = g \cdot x$ for some $g \in G$. This is an equivalence relation on $X$, and its equivalence classes are the orbits. Hence the orbits form a partition of $X$.
:::

:::proof
Reflexivity: $x = e \cdot x$. Symmetry: if $y = g \cdot x$, then $g^{-1} \cdot y = (g^{-1}g) \cdot x = x$. Transitivity: if $y = g \cdot x$ and $z = h \cdot y$, then $z = h \cdot (g \cdot x) = (hg) \cdot x$. The class of $x$ is $\{g \cdot x \mid g \in G\} = G \cdot x$.
:::

:::definition{3.2.6} Faithful and transitive actions
Let $G$ act on $X$, with associated homomorphism $\rho : G \to \Sym(X)$.

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. The ***kernel*** of the action is $\ker\rho = \{g \in G \mid g \cdot x = x \text{ for all } x \in X\}$. The action is ***faithful*** if $\rho$ is injective, that is, if only $e$ acts as the identity on $X$.
2. The action is ***transitive*** if $X \neq \emptyset$ and there is only one orbit: for all $x, y \in X$ there exists $g \in G$ with $g \cdot x = y$.
:::

If an action is not faithful, the group that “really” acts on $X$ is $G/\ker\rho$. Any action of $G$ on $X$ restricts to an action on each orbit, and that action is transitive; so every action is a disjoint union of transitive actions.

:::example{3.2.7} Fundamental examples of group actions
<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. **Permutations:** $S_n$ acts on $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ by $\sigma \cdot i = \sigma(i)$. This action is faithful (the associated homomorphism is the identity of $S_n$) and transitive (the transposition $(i\,j)$ sends $i$ to $j$).
2. **Left multiplication:** $G$ acts on itself by $g \cdot h = gh$. This action is faithful, since $g \cdot e = g$, and transitive, since $(yx^{-1}) \cdot x = y$. Every stabilizer is trivial.
3. **The coset action:** If $H \le G$, then $G$ acts on the set $G/H$ of left cosets by $g \cdot (aH) = (ga)H$. This is well defined: if $aH = a'H$, then $a' = ah$ for some $h \in H$, so $ga'H = gahH = gaH$. The action is transitive, since $(ba^{-1}) \cdot aH = bH$. The stabilizer of $aH$ is $aHa^{-1}$, because $gaH = aH$ if and only if $a^{-1}ga \in H$.
4. **Conjugation:** $G$ acts on itself by $g \cdot h = ghg^{-1}$. This action is the subject of Section [3.2.3](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions) below.
5. **Conjugation on subgroups:** $G$ acts on the set of its subgroups by $g \cdot K = gKg^{-1}$. (The set $gKg^{-1}$ is a subgroup, being the image of $K$ under the homomorphism $h \mapsto ghg^{-1}$ of Section [3.2.3](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions).) The subgroups fixed by every $g \in G$ are exactly the normal subgroups.
6. **Linear actions:** $\GL_n(\RR)$ acts on $\RR^n$ by matrix multiplication, $A \cdot v = Av$. This is the prototype for representation theory.
:::

:::proposition{3.2.8} Stabilizers along an orbit are conjugate
If $y = g \cdot x$, then $\Stab(y) = g\Stab(x)g^{-1}$.
:::

:::proof
If $h \in \Stab(x)$, then $(ghg^{-1}) \cdot y = (ghg^{-1}g) \cdot x = g \cdot (h \cdot x) = g \cdot x = y$, so $g\Stab(x)g^{-1} \subseteq \Stab(y)$. Since $x = g^{-1} \cdot y$, the same argument gives $g^{-1}\Stab(y)g \subseteq \Stab(x)$, that is, $\Stab(y) \subseteq g\Stab(x)g^{-1}$.
:::

## <span class="num">3.2.2</span> The Orbit–Stabilizer Theorem

The following theorem is one of the most useful results in group theory. It says that the action of $G$ on an orbit looks exactly like the coset action of Example [3.2.7](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#example-3-2-7)(c), and it connects the size of an orbit to the index of a stabilizer.

:::theorem{3.2.9} Orbit–Stabilizer Theorem
Let $G$ act on $X$, let $x \in X$, and let $H = \Stab(x)$. The map $$\varepsilon : G/H \to G \cdot x, \qquad aH \mapsto a \cdot x,$$ is a well-defined bijection, and it is ***equivariant***: $\varepsilon(g \cdot aH) = g \cdot \varepsilon(aH)$ for all $g, a \in G$. In particular $|G \cdot x| = [G : \Stab(x)]$, and if $G$ is finite, $$|G \cdot x| = \frac{|G|}{|\Stab(x)|},$$ so the size of every orbit divides $|G|$.
:::

:::proof
**Well defined:** If $aH = bH$, then $b = ah$ for some $h \in H$, so $b \cdot x = a \cdot (h \cdot x) = a \cdot x$.

**Injective:** If $a \cdot x = b \cdot x$, then $(a^{-1}b) \cdot x = a^{-1} \cdot (b \cdot x) = a^{-1} \cdot (a \cdot x) = x$, so $a^{-1}b \in H$ and $aH = bH$.

**Surjective:** Every element of $G \cdot x$ has the form $a \cdot x = \varepsilon(aH)$.

**Equivariant:** $\varepsilon(g \cdot aH) = \varepsilon(gaH) = (ga) \cdot x = g \cdot (a \cdot x) = g \cdot \varepsilon(aH)$.

The counting statements follow from the bijection and Lagrange’s theorem.
:::

:::corollary{3.2.10} Counting orbits
Let a finite group $G$ act on a finite set $X$, and let $x_1, \ldots, x_m$ be one element from each orbit. Then $$|X| = \sum_{i=1}^m |G \cdot x_i| = \sum_{i=1}^m [G : \Stab(x_i)].$$
:::

:::proof
The orbits partition $X$ (Proposition [3.2.5](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#proposition-3-2-5)); now apply the Orbit–Stabilizer Theorem to each orbit.
:::

:::example{3.2.11}
Consider $S_4$ acting on $\{1,2,3,4\}$ in the natural way, and take $x = 1$. The orbit is $S_4 \cdot 1 = \{1,2,3,4\}$, since the action is transitive. The stabilizer $\Stab(1) = \{\sigma \in S_4 \mid \sigma(1) = 1\}$ consists of the permutations of $\{2,3,4\}$, a group isomorphic to $S_3$, so $|\Stab(1)| = 6$. Check: $|S_4 \cdot 1| = 4 = 24/6 = |S_4|/|\Stab(1)|$.
:::

## <span class="num">3.2.3</span> The Conjugation Action and Conjugacy Classes

A group $G$ acts on itself by conjugation, $g \cdot h = ghg^{-1}$. The axioms hold: $e \cdot h = h$, and $$(gg') \cdot h = gg'h(gg')^{-1} = g(g'hg'^{-1})g^{-1} = g \cdot (g' \cdot h).$$ Write $c_g(h) = ghg^{-1}$. Each $c_g$ is a homomorphism, since $c_g(hk) = ghkg^{-1} = (ghg^{-1})(gkg^{-1})$, and a bijection with inverse $c_{g^{-1}}$. So $c_g$ is an automorphism of $G$, and by Proposition [3.2.2](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#proposition-3-2-2) the action is a homomorphism $$c : G \to \Aut(G), \qquad g \mapsto c_g.$$ The automorphisms $c_g$ are called ***inner automorphisms***, and their set $\Inn(G) = \Img c$ is a subgroup of $\Aut(G)$.

:::definition{3.2.12} Conjugacy classes and centralizers
Let $G$ be a group. Two elements $h, h' \in G$ are ***conjugate*** if $h' = ghg^{-1}$ for some $g \in G$. The ***conjugacy class*** of $h$ is its orbit under conjugation, $$C_h = \{ghg^{-1} \mid g \in G\},$$ and the ***centralizer*** of $h$ is its stabilizer, $Z(h) = \{g \in G \mid gh = hg\}$, the subgroup of elements commuting with $h$.
:::

:::proposition{3.2.13} Properties of conjugacy classes
Let $G$ be a group.

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. The conjugacy classes of $G$ form a partition of $G$.
2. $|C_h| = [G : Z(h)]$; if $G$ is finite, $|C_h|$ divides $|G|$.
3. $C_h = \{h\}$ if and only if $h \in Z(G)$. The kernel of the conjugation action is $Z(G)$, so the action is faithful if and only if $Z(G) = \{e\}$.
4. A subgroup $N \le G$ is normal if and only if it is a union of conjugacy classes.
:::

:::proof
(a) is Proposition [3.2.5](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#proposition-3-2-5), and (b) is the Orbit–Stabilizer Theorem, since $Z(h) = \Stab(h)$.

(c) $C_h = \{h\}$ means $ghg^{-1} = h$, that is, $gh = hg$, for all $g$; this says $h \in Z(G)$. An element $g$ is in the kernel when $ghg^{-1} = h$ for all $h$, that is, when $g \in Z(G)$.

(d) If $N$ is normal and $n \in N$, then $C_n = \{gng^{-1}\} \subseteq N$, so $N$ is the union of the classes of its elements. Conversely, if $N$ is a union of conjugacy classes, then $gng^{-1} \in C_n \subseteq N$ for all $n \in N$ and $g \in G$, so $N$ is normal by Proposition [3.1.9](/notes/math-55a/3-1-cosets-and-quotient-groups#proposition-3-1-9).
:::

The conjugacy classes of $S_n$ are described in Section [3.4](/notes/math-55a/3-4-the-symmetric-group), and Chapter 11 builds on this action to prove the class equation and the Sylow theorems.

## <span class="num">3.2.4</span> Cayley’s Theorem

:::theorem{3.2.14} Cayley’s Theorem
Every group $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $\Sym(G)$. If $|G| = n$ is finite, then $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $S_n$.
:::

:::proof
The left multiplication action of $G$ on itself (Example [3.2.7](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#example-3-2-7)(b)) gives a homomorphism $\rho : G \to \Sym(G)$, $\rho(g)(h) = gh$. The action is faithful: if $\rho(g) = \id_G$, then $g = g \cdot e = e$. So $\ker\rho = \{e\}$, $\rho$ is injective, and $G \cong \Img\rho \le \Sym(G)$ (Proposition [2.5.6](/notes/math-55a/2-5-homomorphisms#proposition-2-5-6)).

If $|G| = n$, choose a bijection $\beta : G \to \{1, \ldots, n\}$. Then $\sigma \mapsto \beta\sigma\beta^{-1}$ is an isomorphism $\Sym(G) \to S_n$, with inverse $\tau \mapsto \beta^{-1}\tau\beta$, since $\beta\sigma\sigma'\beta^{-1} = (\beta\sigma\beta^{-1})(\beta\sigma'\beta^{-1})$. Composing gives an injective homomorphism $G \to S_n$.
:::

:::note
Cayley’s theorem is simultaneously profound and useless. Profound: every abstract group is “really” a group of permutations, so the group axioms capture exactly the structure of composition of bijections. Useless: the embedding is almost always far larger than necessary. $S_n$ has order $n!$, so embedding a group of order $n$ into $S_n$ wastes enormous space. Better embeddings come from smaller faithful actions.
:::

The coset action gives such smaller actions. For $H \le G$, the intersection $\bigcap_{a \in G} aHa^{-1}$ is called the ***core*** of $H$ in $G$.

:::proposition{3.2.15} Actions on cosets
Let $H \le G$ with $[G:H] = n$ finite. The action of $G$ on $G/H$ gives a homomorphism $\rho : G \to \Sym(G/H) \cong S_n$ whose kernel is the core $\bigcap_{a \in G} aHa^{-1}$. The core is the largest normal subgroup of $G$ contained in $H$: it is normal, it is contained in $H$, and it contains every normal subgroup of $G$ contained in $H$. In particular, if $H$ contains no normal subgroup of $G$ other than $\{e\}$, then $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $S_n$.
:::

:::proof
The kernel of the action is the set of elements fixing every coset, which is $\bigcap_{a \in G}\Stab(aH) = \bigcap_{a \in G} aHa^{-1}$ by Example [3.2.7](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#example-3-2-7)(c). As a kernel it is normal (Theorem [3.1.10](/notes/math-55a/3-1-cosets-and-quotient-groups#theorem-3-1-10)), and taking $a = e$ shows it is contained in $H$. If $K \trianglelefteq G$ and $K \subseteq H$, then $K = aKa^{-1} \subseteq aHa^{-1}$ for every $a \in G$, so $K$ is contained in the core. For the last statement: the kernel is then $\{e\}$, so $\rho$ is injective and $G$ is isomorphic to its image (Proposition [2.5.6](/notes/math-55a/2-5-homomorphisms#proposition-2-5-6)), a subgroup of $\Sym(G/H) \cong S_n$.
:::

:::example{3.2.16}
<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. Let $G = S_4$ and $H = \Stab(4) \cong S_3$. Then $[G:H] = 4$, and by the Orbit–Stabilizer Theorem the action on $G/H$ is the natural action of $S_4$ on $\{1,2,3,4\}$; here $\rho$ is an isomorphism.
2. Let $G = D_4$, of order 8, and $H = \{e, s\}$ for a reflection $s$, so $[G:H] = 4$. Cayley’s theorem embeds $D_4$ in $S_8$, but we can do better. From $srs^{-1} = r^{-1}$ we get $sr^{-1} = rs$, so $rsr^{-1} = r(sr^{-1}) = r^2s \neq s$. Thus $H \cap rHr^{-1} = \{e, s\} \cap \{e, r^2s\} = \{e\}$, the core of $H$ is trivial, and $D_4$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $S_4$. (If $s$ fixes a vertex of the square, then $H$ is the stabilizer of that vertex, and by the Orbit–Stabilizer Theorem this is the action of $D_4$ on the four vertices.)
:::
